title: Historical introduction to Etruria
paras: Central Italy, 9th-1st centuries BC

Etruria was the first great civilisation of the Italian peninsula and developed between the 9th and 1st centuries BC, from the Villanovan period to the Romano-Etruscan phase, in central Italy, over present-day Tuscany, Lazio and Umbria.

The Etruscans never formed a unitary state, since they were organised into twelve city-states, governed first by kings or great lords and later by magistrates drawn from the aristocracy. Hence a highly polarised society, probably without middle classes.
Etruscan rule over the early Romans lasted a century, between 616 and 509 BC. Rome later absorbed the Etruscan cities, and the independence of Etruria ended in 264 BC.

title: Characteristics of Etruscan sport
paras: Tarquinia, c. 550-400 BC

Sport held a very important place in Etruscan society, which had a deep-rooted physical culture, as shown by the musculature and the athletic bearing of the bodies depicted in its art. Nevertheless, there are no exact data on specific systems of physical education.

The Etruscans, however, left no text about their games, so their sport is known from the outside. What we know comes from a few Greek and Latin texts, from a handful of inscriptions and, above all, from images, which are the main source.

Among these images, the tombs painted with sporting scenes stand out, something very rare in Antiquity outside Egypt. Even so, there were few of them. Of the some six thousand tombs in the necropolis of Tarquinia, only about two hundred bear paintings (around 3%), since decorating a tomb was within the reach of very few families. Between Tarquinia and Chiusi barely seventeen, dated between 530 and 450 BC, show sporting games.

These paintings depict, as studies agree, the funeral games held in honour of the noble deceased who occupies the tomb, like those at the funeral of Patroclus in the Iliad. Painting them on the wall also ensured that the rite was repeated for ever and prolonged its efficacy.
Many of the athletes were professionals in the service of the aristocracy, although the labels in the Tomb of the Inscriptions associate some horsemen with noble families.

title: Etruscan women
paras: Tarquinia, c. 500 BC

The Etruscan woman enjoyed greater freedom than the Greek woman and than the Roman woman would later have, since she took part in feasts and banquets, sometimes as a dancer (right-hand image), and attended sporting events as a spectator.

The Tomb of the Bigae at Tarquinia, painted c. 500 BC, shows the noble spectators seated on wooden stands covered with awnings, men and women together, while the chariots parade before them ahead of the race (image below). In the front row of the stand a woman raises her arm towards the charioteers, a gesture that has been read as a greeting or as the starting signal.
As for practice, there is no evidence that she competed in organised sport, since in the paintings she is never seen taking part in a competition.

title: A clear Greek inspiration
paras: Italy and the Mediterranean, 8th-5th centuries BC
Etruscan sporting scenes closely resemble those of the great Greek festivals, since Greek sport reached Italy from the south.
From the mid-8th century BC the Greeks founded cities in southern Italy and in Sicily, and in them people trained and competed as in Greece.
Objects also arrived with trade. Etruscan tombs are full of Panathenaic amphorae, the prizes of the games of Athens, like the one in the image, which reached Etruria as an imported luxury.

The Etruscans also knew the Greek sanctuaries. They built a treasury at Delphi, and an Etruscan king was the first foreigner to make an offering to Zeus at Olympia, although there is no evidence that any Etruscan competed in the Greek games.

title: Athletics, wrestling and boxing
paras: The Etruscans took over a good part of the Greek events and did different things with them. In athletics the form of the events remained almost intact, whereas in wrestling and boxing the Greek element was added to a tradition of their own that already existed.

Athletics. The Etruscans adopted many Olympic events, such as running, discus throwing, javelin or the long jump, which was performed, as in Greece, with halteres. A figure in the Tomb of the Bigae has also been read as a pole vault. What was being jumped over is unknown, although Thuillier (1985) suggests that the pole might have served to vault over a horse.
Tarquinia, 6th-5th centuries BC

Wrestling and boxing. They combined Greek influence with a tradition of their own, since there were already Etruscan boxers in the 7th century BC. Boxing was the favourite sport of the Etruscans, and it almost always appears accompanied by a flute player, who according to Thuillier (2013) set the rhythm of the fight, whereas Greek authors took him for a sign of softness. The depictions show well-trained wrestlers. In the Tomb of the Augurs (image below) two wrestlers compete for the three bronze cauldrons that were the prize.

title: Aquatic activities
paras: Tarquinia, late 6th century BC

In the Tomb of Hunting and Fishing at Tarquinia, one of the most famous in the necropolis, a youth dives headfirst into the sea from a rock, while another climbs up it (image). The scene was painted at the end of the 6th century BC.

The meaning of the dive is debated. For a similar scene, that of the young man plunging into the water in the Tomb of the Diver at Paestum, a symbolic reading has been proposed, the passage of the soul of the deceased from the world of the living to the afterlife (Bellia, 2014). Hölscher (2022), by contrast, reads it as a physical practice of elite youths that marked their coming of age. For the tomb at Tarquinia, Thuillier (1985) considers that the symbolic reading has no foundation and that it would simply show young people enjoying themselves and spending some leisure time in the water.

The Etruscans were, indeed, a people who mastered the aquatic environment. They were seafarers, devoted to trade, fishing and, according to Greek authors, piracy, so swimming may well have been a common practice among them. Even so, no Etruscan document allows us to speak of competitions in the water.

title: Etruscan chariot racing
paras: Chiusi and Tarquinia, 6th-5th centuries BC
Chariot racing was one of the favourite activities of the Etruscans, who preferred the biga to the quadriga and also used the triga, the three-horse chariot.

The Etruscan charioteer differed from the Greek one in three ways. He tied the reins around his waist, which multiplied the risk in the event of an accident, but allowed him to drive with one hand. With the other he wielded the whip, instead of the long goad with which the Greek urged on the horses. Finally, he wore a short tunic and a helmet, as opposed to the long tunic and bare head of the Greek charioteer.

The social origin of the charioteers is disputed. Crowther and Kyle consider them to be of servile origin (cited in Banducci, 2014) and Thuillier (1985), low-ranking professionals dependent on a lord, although Banducci (2014) warns that there is no proof.

The audience was the aristocracy, and since keeping horses and charioteers was very expensive, the race displayed the wealth of whoever paid for it. What Etruscan art repeats again and again is the crash, the overturned chariot and the charioteer flying through the air, which for the public was the most exciting moment, something that anticipates the taste for violence in sport that the Romans would inherit.

title: Horse racing and the troia
paras: Murlo and Tragliatella, 7th-6th centuries BC

Horse races with riders are documented above all on the terracotta plaques of Murlo, c. 600 BC, and afterwards they are hardly ever depicted again. The image shows an Etruscan bit of c. 700-650 BC, the metal piece placed in the horse's mouth which, joined to the reins, makes it possible to guide the mount.
Their place was taken by the desultores, acrobatic riders who leapt from one horse to another in mid-race. Etruscan horsemanship thus moved from racing to acrobatics.
The troia was another equestrian discipline, a game of skill on horseback in which the riders followed a labyrinth of curves, as shown by the jug from the 7th century BC in the image.

title: The phersu and the gladiators
paras: Tarquinia, c. 530 BC

The Tomb of the Augurs at Tarquinia, painted c. 530 BC, shows a masked figure with his name written above his head, the phersu, which probably means «mask» and is related to the Latin persona. The phersu sets a dog on a hooded man who holds a club to defend himself, but the rope held by the masked figure prevents him from saving his life.

The meaning of the scene remains open. Thuillier (1985) sees the phersu as an executioner putting a condemned man to death, in a punishment closer to condemnation to the beasts than to gladiatorial combat, whereas Avramidou (2009) interprets it as the staging of an Orphic rite, with the masked figure in the role of Orpheus and the dog in that of Cerberus. Orpheus was the musician of Greek mythology who went down to the world of the dead to rescue his wife, and Cerberus the three-headed dog that guarded its entrance, so the scene would represent the passage of the soul of the deceased to the afterlife.

For a long time this scene was regarded as the direct precedent of gladiatorial games. However, none of the seventeen paintings of funeral games from Tarquinia and Chiusi shows a single gladiator, and gladiatorial combat did not reach Etruria until the late 4th or early 3rd century BC, so the phersu remains, at most, a forerunner of the combats with wild beasts (Kyle, 1998).

title: Etruscan games
paras: The social life of the Etruscan upper classes included numerous feasts and banquets, and at these gatherings it was customary to play games in which wine took centre stage.

Three of these games stood out. In the ascolia one had to keep one's balance on a greased wineskin (a sheepskin bag), and in the kottabos the last drops in the cup were flung at a target, such as the dish of a candelabrum (right-hand image). People also played dice, probably for stakes.
Nevertheless, these games were only partly Etruscan, since kottabos is documented at the Greek banquet. Dice were also played by aristocratic women.

title: What Rome inherited from Etruria
paras: Etruria and Rome, 7th-3rd centuries BC

Etruscan sport faded out before Etruria itself. Scenes of games disappear from the tombs at the end of the 5th century BC, and the last is that of the Tomb of the Warrior, c. 400 BC, probably because keeping athletes and charioteers was very expensive and the aristocracy had grown poorer.

What Rome received from Etruscan sport was, above all, the preference of the nobility for attending as spectators. In Etruria the aristocracy watched and the competing fell to paid professionals. The Roman social elites inherited that position, since they shared the sense of shame at performing before the public as professional athletes (Thuillier, 2013).

The legacy can also be seen in the equestrian programme. According to Livy, the first Etruscan king of Rome (Tarquinius Priscus) brought horses and boxers mainly from Etruria, and Rome kept the triga, the desultores, the troia and the reins tied around the waist, which its charioteers used until the end of the Empire. The wooden stands with awnings of the Tomb of the Bigae also match what ancient historians tell us about the first stands of the Circus Maximus.

title: Historical introduction to Rome
paras: The history of Rome spans more than twelve centuries, from its foundation as a small city in Latium to the fall of the Western Empire, and it is usually divided into three stages according to who held power, namely the Monarchy, the Republic and the Empire.

Monarchy (753-509 BC). According to tradition, Rome was founded in 753 BC. Its first system of government lay with kings, the last three of them Etruscans, until in 509 BC the aristocracy expelled the last of them, Tarquinius Superbus, whom tradition presents as a tyrant. Today it is understood as a reaction by the great lineages to recover the power that the kings had taken from them, at a time when Etruscan rule was receding in Latium.

Republic (509-27 BC). The aristocracy divided the power of the king between two consuls elected every year, who could veto each other, so that no one would ever again rule alone. In those centuries Rome conquered Italy and, after defeating Carthage in the Punic Wars, the rest of the Mediterranean, until the civil wars of the 1st century BC, in which generals at the head of their own armies fought one another, brought the republican system to an end. The most powerful of them, Julius Caesar, had himself appointed dictator for life and was assassinated in 44 BC.

Empire (27 BC-AD 476). It began with Augustus, Caesar's great-nephew and adopted son, who concentrated all power without abolishing the republican institutions and was the first of more than seventy emperors. On the death of Theodosius, in AD 395, it was divided between his two sons, Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West, because such a vast territory was very difficult to govern from a single centre. The western half, under pressure from the 3rd century onwards from the Germanic peoples crossing its frontiers, suffered the sack of Rome by the Visigoths in AD 410 and fell in AD 476, when a Germanic chieftain, Odoacer, deposed the last emperor, while the eastern half, with its capital at Constantinople, survived for almost a thousand years more.

title: Governing Rome, from Republic to Empire
paras: Rome, 509 BC-3rd century AD

The chart compares the government of Rome under the Republic (upper half) and under the Empire (lower half), level by level, from supreme power, at the centre, to the people, in the outer ring. At the centre of the Republic were the two consuls, elected every year, and around them the Senate, which brought together for life some 300 former magistrates and decided on war, taxes and the government of the provinces.

The magistrates were the public officials elected to govern Rome, that is, to command the armies, administer justice and run the life of the city. Among them were the aediles, in charge of the markets, public buildings and festivals. Each office was held by at least two people who could veto each other and received no pay, so only the rich could afford them. As they were elected every year by the citizens' vote, anyone who aspired to an office needed to win over the people.

In the outer ring, the assemblies brought together male citizens to elect the magistrates and vote on laws, although voting was by groups according to wealth. After a long struggle with the old patrician families, the plebeians also won their own representatives, the tribunes of the plebs, who could veto any magistrate.

Augustus kept these institutions, although he left them without real power. He himself occupied the centre as princeps, «first citizen», for life, with command of all the armies and the powers of the tribunes. The Senate, with some 600 members purged by the emperor, governed only the pacified provinces. The magistrates, now elected by the Senate, kept only the prestige of the title, and positions of trust passed to the equites, the second group of the elite. The assemblies disappeared in the 1st century AD, so the people stopped voting and could make itself heard only in the circus, the theatre and the amphitheatre (Woolf, 2012).

title: The Roman social pyramid
paras: Rome, 2nd century BC-2nd century AD

Roman society in the age of the great spectacles was ordered by wealth and rank, and the chart represents it as a pyramid. At the top, below the emperor, were the two orders of the elite: the senatorial, made up of the few families that controlled the government, the army and the provinces, and the equestrian, that of the equites, so called because they originally served on horseback in the army. Over time, the equestrian order brought together businessmen and senior administrators, with a smaller fortune than the senators and no access to the Senate. After them came the notables of each city, who governed their community from the local council.

The dashed line separates the powerful from the humble, a boundary that the law used to grade punishments, so that the cruellest penalties, such as death before the wild beasts, were reserved for this social stratum. The largest group among them was the plebs, the free citizens without fortune.

At the base were the slaves, the private property of their masters and without rights. Most were prisoners of war, so this was not a racial slavery, although people were also enslaved for debts or crimes. Manumission, that is, release by the master, turned them into freedmen, who became citizens, although with a lower rank than the freeborn. Their children, on the other hand, were born free and without that mark.

title: Roman women
paras: Rome, 1st century BC-2nd century AD

The Roman woman occupied a secondary position, since she lacked political rights, so she did not vote in the assemblies or hold a magistracy, and she depended legally on her father or her husband. Her situation, however, varied greatly according to her class.

The woman of the elite was exempt from work, apart from household tasks, and was expected to behave with moral rectitude, an image of composure conveyed by portraits such as the one on the right, of a woman of the family of Augustus. Widows enjoyed greater freedom. The women of the plebs, by contrast, worked in shops, workshops and markets, so a woman's free time, like a man's, depended on having someone to work for her.

Unlike the Etruscan woman, who attended banquets and competitions alongside men, the Roman woman had her presence in public restricted, and at the spectacles too. She could attend them, although with limitations, and Augustus went as far as forbidding women to attend his contests of Greek athletes, apparently because of the nudity of the athletes.

title: From agon to ludus
paras: Greece and Rome, 5th century BC-2nd century AD

There was a great difference between Greek and Roman sport. For the classical Greeks what mattered was the competition between the participants, whereas in Rome spectacle came above everything else. The Greek agon was the contest with an opponent, and the Roman ludus, the game offered to the public. Although it was originally linked to religious activities, Roman sport soon evolved into a public spectacle and an instrument of political power. The image of that spectacle we have today owes much to 19th-century paintings such as Gérôme's (left-hand image).
Sport in Rome was characterised by:
The perception of sport as public entertainment.
A contempt for the lives of others and a taste for violence.
The emergence of sporting professionalism and financial gain.
The development of large-scale sports facilities to favour display.
The use of sport as political control of the plebs.
The active role of the spectators during events.

title: Ludi and munera
paras: The words of Roman spectacle

The Romans had no term equivalent to our «sport», and for their games they used two words that designated different things, the ludi (plural of ludus) and the munera, each with its own origin, its own calendar and its own payer.

1. Ludi. These were the public games of the religious calendar, offered to the gods and originally paid for by the State, and they included the chariot races of the circus (ludi circenses) and theatrical performances (ludi scaenici).

2. Munus. The word meant both «duty» and «gift». Originally it was a son's obligation to his dead father, whom he honoured with a gladiatorial combat, and around the beginning of the Empire it came to designate above all the combat that a private individual offered to the people.

The difference between the two terms marked who decided. The ludi were public festivals with a fixed date, whereas the munus depended on the will and the purse of whoever offered it, as shown by the bags of money paid by Magerius in the mosaic on the right.

title: «Bread and circuses»
paras: Rome, 3rd century BC-4th century AD
DAYS OF PUBLIC GAMES PER YEAR
Age of Augustus  ·  27 BC-AD 14

To stage the spectacles, the authorities invested a great amount of resources in building spaces capable of hosting major sporting events. This was the policy of «bread and circuses» (panem et circenses), according to which Romans were to have access to affordable food, such as the public grain, which covered around 40% of a family's basic food (Toner, 2014), and to public entertainments with which those in power won their favour.
The expression comes from the satirical poet Juvenal, who in the 2nd century AD used it as a reproach to the plebs, which once handed out commands and legions and now wanted only bread and races.

The days of public games multiplied over the course of the Empire, from 65 in the age of Augustus (27 BC-AD 14) and 80 in that of Tiberius (AD 14-37) to 176 in the calendar of AD 354, which brought together the festivals accumulated over centuries. Of these, some 102 were for theatre, 64 for races in the circus and only 10 for gladiators (see chart). Each of these spectacles rested on the same system, that is, on who paid for them, who competed and who watched.

title: Who paid for the spectacles
paras: Sporting spectacles were free for the public, and their cost fell on those who sought something in return, above all the favour of the people. Who paid for them also changed with the political regime (see charts).

Under the Republic, the games of the calendar were the responsibility of the magistrates, especially the aediles, who paid for them with public money to which they usually added their own, and for them they were an «extraordinary opportunity for electoral propaganda», since the people who enjoyed them were the same people who voted for them (Roldán, 1990).

Under the Empire, the emperor became the great sponsor. In Rome he sought to reserve the great spectacles for himself, while in the provinces they continued to be paid for by the magistrates of each city (Scheidel et al., 2007).

title: The emperor in the stands
paras: Rome and Constantinople, 1st-4th centuries AD

What the emperor obtained in return for paying for the games could be seen in the stands. He attended the great spectacles and his presence was part of the spectacle, since from the imperial box he showed himself as the one who gave the games, as an intermediary between the city and the gods and as the arbiter who granted or refused what was asked of him. In the image, Theodosius presides over the games from the imperial box of the hippodrome of Constantinople, surrounded by his court.

As the people no longer voted, the stands were the place where they could make demands. The public took advantage of the emperor's presence to clamour for, for example, a reduction in taxes, and he answered there and then before tens of thousands of witnesses, so that each answer strengthened or wore down his prestige.
What he offered in the arena served the same end. Titus and Trajan exhibited there the delatores, the professional informers whom the people hated, and thus gave the public what it asked for.

title: 4.2.3. The amphitheatre, gladiators and other games
Amphitheatre
paras: The Roman amphitheatre was a public building with an elliptical plan, with stands all around its perimeter surrounding a central space covered with sand (harena), which gave its name to the place of combat.

The first amphitheatres arose from joining two theatres facing each other, so that the stands completely surrounded the spectacle and the arena could be seen from any seat. They were made of wood, like the one in the Roman Forum in the reconstruction in the image, and later they were built in stone, brick and even marble, the largest reaching three or four tiers of stands one above the other.

The public entered through the vomitoria, the vaulted arches that gave access to the stands, and these rose several metres above the arena to protect the spectators from the fighters and the wild beasts.

title: Flavian Amphitheatre
paras: Colosseum
Rome, AD 72-80

The Flavian Amphitheatre, today called the Colosseum, was built between AD 72 and 80 under the Flavian dynasty. The emperor Vespasian began the works and his son Titus inaugurated it after his death with a hundred days of games.
It is one of the masterpieces of Roman architecture, and its design inspired many later amphitheatres. Its four tiers of stands surrounded an arena of some 80 by 54 metres.

Beneath the arena lay a network of corridors, cells and lifts for bringing out gladiators and wild beasts, and above the stands an enormous awning (velarium) was stretched, operated by sailors from the fleet.

The remains of its inscription suggest that it was paid for with the spoils of the Judaean war and the plunder of the Temple of Solomon, which is why it was at once a victory monument and a gift to the people.

title: The ordered stands
paras: Rome, from Augustus onwards

The amphitheatre audience did not sit wherever it wished. The lex Iulia theatralis, a law of Augustus, allocated the seats of theatres and amphitheatres by social group, so that the stands reproduced the hierarchy of the city.

The allocation ran from bottom to top. The emperor occupied his box, the senators the front rows next to the arena, the equites the following ones and behind them the rest of the citizens in togas, while women, slaves and foreigners were left at the very top. The Vestals, priestesses of the goddess Vesta, were the only female exception.

The figures for the Colosseum make it possible to measure that allocation (see chart). Bomgardner (2000) estimates that senators, equites and citizens in togas (free men with civic rights) held 62% of the seats, women 19% and the poor, slaves, freedmen and foreigners 18%, which were the worst.
The dissignatores, the ushers of the amphitheatre, prevented a plebeian from occupying the reserved rows, which is why going to the games meant seeing and being seen, each in his place.

title: Gladiatorial combats
paras: Munera gladiatoria · Rome, 264 BC-AD 107

Gladiatorial combats reached Rome from Campania, in southern Italy, where they were part of the funerals of the aristocracy. The first documented in the city of Rome dates from 264 BC, when the sons of a nobleman offered a munus in honour of their dead father and set three pairs of slaves against each other in the Forum Boarium, the cattle market beside the Tiber.

During the Republic the combats grew at the pace of political competition. In 105 BC one of the consuls brought in the trainers of a gladiatorial school to drill his soldiers in the use of the sword, and candidates for office kept increasing the number of pairs to win over the people. Julius Caesar presented 320 pairs as aedile, in 65 BC, and the Senate, alarmed by the number of armed men he had gathered in the city, limited the number of gladiators a private individual could own.

The peak came with the Empire, when the emperor took control of the combats in Rome. Augustus limited those offered by the magistrates to two a year and to 120 gladiators each, so that the great munera remained in the emperor's hands. The games of Trajan for his victory in Dacia (present-day Romania), in AD 107, lasted 123 days and brought together some ten thousand gladiators.

title: Gladiators and infamia
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st century BC-2nd century AD

Gladiators came from three groups. Slaves were bought for the arena or hired out by their owners, and the condemned could be sentenced ad gladium, to die in the arena, or ad ludum, to go to the school and learn the trade. Finally, free men sold themselves to a lanista, the entrepreneur who bought, trained and hired out gladiators, by means of a contract, the auctoramentum, and swore to accept «being burned, chained, beaten and killed by the sword».

All of them shared infamia, a legal and moral stain that the law imposed on those who sold or displayed their bodies for the enjoyment of others. The infamis could not vote, hold a magistracy, testify in a trial or contract a legal marriage, and what stained was displaying oneself for money. For this reason, in AD 19 a decree of the Senate punished senators and equites who sought to fight in the arena.

Even so, infamia coexisted with admiration. Epitaphs present the gladiator with the courage, the prestige and the comradeship of the champion, and the people treated him as a hero «at once famous and infamous» (Bell, 2020).

title: The life of gladiators
paras: Gladiators lived and trained in the ludus, a school run by a lanista. The largest was that of Capua, in southern Italy, which came to house up to 5,000 gladiators. In Rome, Domitian built next to the Colosseum the Ludus Magnus (right-hand image), the main imperial school, with a small arena for training surrounded by stands and, apparently, connected to the amphitheatre by an underground passage.
The volunteer signed up for the agreed period and number of fights. Each gladiator received a combat identity (armatura), with a specific set of offensive and defensive weapons.

The training included a physical part (endurance, speed, strength, reflexes) and a specific part with weapons, against a wooden post and later with blunt weapons, supervised by retired veterans. Combat weapons were kept in the armamentarium and were handed out only for combat. The school also had baths, masseurs and medical care.

The relationship with the lanista was, above all, economic. The gladiator paid nothing for his food, lodging or training, which were borne by the lanista, and in return the latter kept most of what he earned. A law of AD 177 laid down that the gladiator should receive a quarter of what the lanista was paid for his fight if he was free and a fifth if he was a slave.

title: Wives, children and comrades
paras: Roman West, 1st-3rd centuries AD
Gladiators formed families even though they could not marry legally. In Hispania, some 40% of the known dead had a wife, half of them freeborn or freed.
Tombstones remember them with the same formulae as any Roman family, and on them wives, children and comrades dedicated the epitaph with the affection usual in the rest of society.

Fellow members of the school also formed a community of their own. Like many humble Romans, some gladiators joined associations which, in return for a fee, guaranteed them a decent burial, and sometimes it was the troupe itself that paid for the tomb of a dead comrade.

The money came from the summa honoraria, the fee paid by whoever took up an office, from what the editor added out of his own pocket and from the city's funds. title: The combats
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st century BC-2nd century AD

A munus was announced in advance on painted notices on the walls of the city, the edicta munerum. The day followed a fixed order that built up from less to more, with the wild-beast hunts (venationes) in the morning, the execution of the condemned at midday and, in the afternoon, the main and most expensive act, the gladiatorial combats, which unfolded in six steps.
1. The eve. The night before, a great dinner open to the public was held, the cena libera, at which the gladiators could break their diet of training.
2. The entrance. The following day they paraded into the arena up to the box of the editor.
3. The inspection of the weapons. In the probatio armorum the weapons were checked and the pairs confirmed, which set different types against each other or, in some types, identical gladiators.
4. The combat. The referee, the summa rudis, watched over the duel, which lasted between 10 and 15 minutes according to Junkelmann's (2000) tests with replicas of the equipment.

5. The verdict. The loser dropped his shield and raised his index finger to ask for mercy, and the editor, attentive to the stands, decided between missio, reprieve, and iugula, the cutting of the throat.
6. The exit. The fallen left the arena for the store for the bodies, where, according to Kyle (1998), they were probably routinely finished off.

title: The wooden sword
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st-3rd centuries AD

A gladiator could leave the trade by two different routes. The first was discharge, symbolised by the rudis, a wooden sword used for training. The gladiator who received it, the rudiarius, was exempted from fighting, although if he was a slave he remained one and could stay on at the school.

The second was freedom, manumissio, which changed his legal status and made him a freedman, although it did not free him from infamia. In the case of those condemned to the school, according to the jurist Ulpian, discharge came after three years and freedom after five.

Discharged gladiators did not always retire. Their fame allowed them to return to the arena at the request of the organiser and the public, and those who were already free then fought as professionals.

Some veterans ended up as referees. The chief referee, the summa rudis, and his assistant, the secunda rudis, enforced the rules and separated the fighters with a rod. Their authority extended beyond the arena, since some young men of Paestum, in southern Italy, honoured a freedman in the mid-3rd century AD as «their» summa rudis, a sign that he also taught arms to the youth of the city.

title: Types of gladiator (I)
paras: Murmillo

Short sword, large rectangular shield and a helmet with a fish-shaped crest, which made him recognisable at a glance. He waited behind his shield until he could deliver the decisive blow, never fought another murmillo and is the type most frequent on the tombstones of the West, with 29 cases.
Thracian (thraex)

Short curved sword (sica), small shield (parma) and two high greaves. He owed his name to the Thracian warriors and reached Rome around the eighties of the 1st century BC, with Sulla's prisoners. Against the murmillo he formed the most popular pairing of the arena.
Hoplomachus

Inspired by the Greek hoplite, he carried a spear, a short sword, a small round shield of bronze and greaves up to mid-thigh. He attacked at a distance with the spear and faced the murmillo and, at times, the Thracian, with whom he is confused because of the similar helmet.
Fans were divided between supporters of the small shield (parmularii) and of the large one (scutarii), and even emperors took sides, Caligula with the former and Domitian with the latter.

title: Types of gladiator (II)
paras: Secutor

Smooth full helmet, with eyeholes barely three centimetres across, a large shield and 16-18 kg of equipment. His name comes from sequor, «to follow», because he pursued the retiarius without letting him cast his net, although he tired sooner. The epitaph of Flamma, a Syrian secutor, records 34 fights, with 21 victories.
Retiarius

A light gladiator, without a shield and bare-faced, with a net, trident and dagger and 7-8 kg of equipment. He retreated and circled his opponent until he gained the distance for the throw. He was one of the stars of the programme, to the point that opponents were created to suit him.
Scissor

He put his left hand into a metal cone ending in a half-moon blade, which served him both as a shield and as a weapon to cut the net. At 22 to 26 kg, he was the heaviest, although it is a poorly known type and his weight comes from modern reconstructions.
Inscriptions abbreviate the secutor's pairing as contra ret, «against the retiarius», so common was it.

title: Types of gladiator (III)
paras: Provocator
Large shield and a breastplate over the chest (cardiophylax), with 14-15 kg. He fought against another provocator, which is why his fights were very evenly matched.
Horseman (eques)
On horseback, with a spear and a round shield, only against another eques. He brought his opponent down with the spear and finished him off on foot, and the programme usually opened with them.
Essedarius
On the light chariot of the Britons, against another essedarius. He was introduced after Caesar's campaigns in Britain (55-54 BC), and the tombstones of the West record eight.
Archer (sagittarius)
An archer with a bow of 150 to 200 metres range, which made it necessary to protect the public. He fought against other archers and was a minority type.
A case apart, the dimachaerus (dimachaerus)
Two machetes and no shield. A programme from Pompeii announces him against a hoplomachus, and it is debated whether he was a type of his own or a way of fighting.

title: Female gladiators and huntresses
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st-3rd centuries AD

The presence of women in the arena was rare, and seeing a woman perform in public was so shocking for the Romans that each one was exhibited as a curiosity. The term gladiatrix is modern, and literary sources mention them fewer than ten times up to the year AD 200.

The key piece is the relief from Halicarnassus, in present-day Turkey, reproduced in the image. In it two women armed as gladiators, Amazon and Achillia, face each other bare-faced, and the inscription says that both were reprieved, an ending so rare that it deserved to be remembered.

What scandalised the Romans was, according to Coleman (2000), rank rather than sex. A rule of AD 11 barred free women under the age of twenty from the arena, and ancient authors condemn only those of senatorial or equestrian family.
Female beast hunters were better accepted because they evoked Diana, the goddess of hunting, according to Mañas (2026). Even so, in the year 200 an imperial decree forbade all women to fight.

title: Venationes
paras: Rome and the provinces, 2nd century BC-6th century AD
The venationes were amphitheatre spectacles with animals such as deer, wild boar or dogs and wild beasts such as lions, elephants or bears, brought from every corner of the empire.

The animals were captured by professional hunters or specialised companies. Sometimes they were captured by the emperor's guard on his direct orders, or they were given by foreign monarchs, such as the king of Mauretania who gave 100 lions to the dictator Sulla.
There were four forms.
1. Display. Exotic beasts were presented to the public and sometimes performed trained.
2. Fights between beasts. The organisers set some animals against others.
3. Hunts. Armed men (venatores) hunted the beasts or fought against them (bestiarii).
4. Executions. Those condemned to the beasts (damnati ad bestias) died in the arena.

The meat of the animals was probably shared out among the spectators. At the inauguration of the Colosseum, in AD 80, 5,000 animals died in a single day, and in the games of Trajan in AD 107, some 11,000.

title: Naumachiae
paras: Rome, 46 BC-AD 80

Naumachiae were naval battles staged with warships and thousands of combatants, almost always condemned men, on lakes or in basins dug for the occasion. The first was organised by Julius Caesar in 46 BC, beside the Tiber, and that of Augustus, in 2 BC, was held in a pool of 533 by 355 metres on the other bank of the river, an area equivalent, allowing for the differences, to some twenty-five football pitches. The largest recorded was that of Claudius on Lake Fucinus, in central Italy, in AD 52, with 19,000 men. At the inauguration of the Colosseum, in AD 80, the arena was flooded for another, although with scale-model ships and fewer participants.

The combats recreated historical battles between Greeks, Persians, Phoenicians or Egyptians. None of the known ones featured a Roman fleet, something Coleman (1993) attributes to the risk that the outcome might not be the expected one. Their enormous cost also reserved them for exceptional occasions, such as a triumph or the inauguration of a building, so very few were held.

title: Circus
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st century BC-4th century AD

The circus was the venue for chariot races, although it also hosted, on occasion, wild-beast hunts. Only the main cities of the Empire built one, since it required an esplanade several hundred metres long and an expense that few communities could bear. Outside Rome more than fifty are known, several of them in Hispania, such as that of Mérida. Together with the amphitheatre and the theatre, it formed the triad of great buildings with which cities entertained the people.

The races reached Rome from Greece by way of Etruria, and Rome transformed them. In Greece they were a competition between aristocrats, won by the owner of the horses, whereas in Rome they became a spectacle that the magistrates, and later the emperor, offered to the people, with professional charioteers. For that public a new building arose (Humphrey, 1986), since the Greek hippodrome, even at Olympia, was an esplanade with earth embankments, and the circus surrounded the track with built stands.

The diagram on the right shows a very elongated enclosure, with one straight end and one curved end. At the straight end were the starting gates (carceres), and at the curved end, the triumphal gate (porta triumphalis). Along the axis ran a low wall, the spina, which divided the track in two, and at each of its ends stood the metae, conical columns that marked the turning points of the chariots.

title: Circus Maximus
paras: Rome, 6th century BC-6th century AD

The Circus Maximus was the largest building for spectacles in Rome. It occupied the valley between the Aventine and the Palatine (two of the hills of Rome), so that at first the public followed the races from the slopes. Tradition attributes to the Etruscan kings the first stands, which were made of wood.

The venue was monumentalised over the centuries. Julius Caesar enlarged it in 46 BC, Augustus raised on the spina an Egyptian obelisk that now stands in the Piazza del Popolo, and Trajan rebuilt it in stone at the beginning of the 2nd century AD.

In imperial times it measured some 620 metres long by 140 wide, and its twelve carceres made it possible to line up twelve chariots. Its capacity was 150,000 spectators according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Greek historian of the 1st century BC), a figure that Pliny the Elder (Roman naturalist of the 1st century AD) raises to 250,000. Allowing for the differences, the first figure almost doubles the capacity of the Santiago Bernabéu, which is around 83,000.

title: Chariot racing
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st-4th centuries AD

In Rome the races were presided over by the emperor, from a box next to the statues of the gods, with the plebs in the stands. Each chariot raced in the colour of its team. Quadrigae (4 horses) almost always raced, although there were also bigae (2) and trigae (3), and races with up to ten horses are known.

The charioteer drove with the reins tied around his waist, so that he controlled the chariot with the weight of his body, although he ran the risk of being dragged if it overturned. That risk explains the knife he carried to cut the reins. The rest of his equipment protected him from falls, with a padded helmet, a thick tunic with leather bands across the chest and bandages on the legs (fasciae crurales).

The start was given by whoever paid for the games, who from a platform above the carceres dropped a white cloth, the mappa. The chariots left the gates, which were arranged in an arc so that none started with an advantage, and kept to their lane up to a white line. Then they all sought the inside line, next to the spina, the shortest route. They ran seven laps, with thirteen turns and some 5 km, in eight or nine minutes and at some 35 km/h according to Bell (2020).

The race was decided at the turns, where the charioteer hugged the metae, and on the inside line, where drivers tried to block their rivals. Hugging them too closely or colliding with another chariot caused the crashes (naufragia, «shipwrecks»).

title: The circus factions
paras: Rome, 1st century BC-4th century AD

The circus factions were the companies which, from the beginning of the Empire or perhaps from the end of the Republic, organised the racing teams. Each one was identified with a colour, white, red, green or blue, to which Domitian added for a time gold and purple, and the word factio designated that colour and its stables, not the groups of fans. In each race a faction could enter up to three chariots to block the path of the rivals of its best charioteer.

At the head of each was its owner (dominus factionis), a businessman of the order of the equites. The factions arose as independent agents, and in the last centuries of the Empire they came under the control of the emperor.

Each faction maintained several hundred employees. In the familia of the Reds twelve trades are documented, among them the conditor, who looked after and fed the horses, the morator, who held them at the start, the sparsor, who cooled them down during the race, the medicus, the doctor, and the sutor, the shoemaker. Their stables, the stabula, were in the city itself, and the horses came from private and imperial stud farms in Hispania, Sicily, Thessaly, North Africa and Cappadocia.

title: How a faction worked
paras: Whoever paid for the games negotiated with the dominus factionis the price of each day, and in return the faction hired out to him the horses, the charioteers and the equipment (see chart). The organiser also bore the cost of the prizes, of some 20,000 sesterces for each quadriga victory, more than fourteen years of a legionary's pay (Vamplew, 2023).

The business was enormous, since in the mid-4th century AD Rome held some 66 days of racing a year, with 24 races per day (Bell, 2020). As there were only four factions and no organiser could give games without them, their owners came to impose their own terms.

Under Nero they refused to hire out the teams except for whole days, so the organiser had to pay for the entire day even if he wanted fewer races. When one of them threatened to race dogs instead of horses, the Reds and the Whites gave in, while the Blues and the Greens held out until the emperor himself paid the prizes (Cameron, 1976).

title: Charioteers and their fortunes
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st-2nd centuries AD

Charioteers were slaves, freedmen or Romans of very low status, and of the more than two hundred known from their inscriptions only one is recorded as freeborn. The best became idols of the masses with statues in Rome, and those who reached a thousand victories formed the group of the miliarii, with barely four names.

The best-known case is that of Diocles, a freedman from Lusitania who raced for twenty-four years, from AD 122 to 146, in 4,257 races, with 1,462 victories, and retired at the age of forty-two. His inscription, an account balance in stone, adds up to 35,863,120 sesterces in prizes, almost thirty-six times the senatorial census (a fortune of one million sesterces) and the pay of a legionary for more than 25,000 years.

That sum, however, did not all end up in his pocket. The prize was collected by the faction, owner of the horses and the chariot, and the charioteer received only a share, which a slave could save in order to buy his freedom. Vamplew (2023) calculates that Diocles kept at least three and a half million, a tenth of the total, and even so Bell (2014) considers him perhaps the best-paid sportsman in history.
Other charioteers started very young and did not live to enjoy their fortune. Crescens won his first race at thirteen, and Scorpus died at twenty-seven after more than two thousand victories.

title: Betting and cursing
paras: Rome, Hispania and North Africa, 1st-4th centuries AD
Passion for the circus was also measured in money. In the stands people bet, and the poet Juvenal censures a magistrate who lost his fortune betting at the very games he was organising.
Fans also tried to draw luck towards their charioteer with rings and amulets bearing his image or the colour of his faction, sometimes with the cry of the stands, NICA, «win!».

Others commissioned misfortune for their rivals by means of curse tablets (defixiones), lead sheets inscribed by magicians that were almost always deposited in tombs, because it was believed that the dead carried the request to the gods of the underworld. One from North Africa asks that the rival horses «may not be able to run, nor obey the bit, nor move», and that their charioteers «may not hold the reins nor see their opponents». The only one found in Hispania, at Écija and dating from the 1st century AD, curses one by one thirteen chariots of the Blues and the Reds (Sánchez Natalías, 2022).

title: Baths
paras: Rome and the provinces, 1st century BC-4th century AD

The thermae were bathhouses in which bathing was combined with physical exercise. There were public and private ones, and the great imperial baths of Rome were decorated with marbles, statues and even libraries, like those of Caracalla.

The separation of the sexes changed over time. The oldest baths, such as those of Pompeii, had two sets of rooms, one for each sex, whereas the great imperial baths had only one, and other baths set different timetables. At the mine of Vipasca (Portugal, 2nd century AD), women bathed in the morning and men in the afternoon. Even so, Ward (1992) finds mixed bathing up to the 4th century.

The baths served for hygiene, relaxation and socialising. Entry cost a quadrans, the smallest coin, so anyone could afford it, and for the ordinary Roman the bath was both spa and meeting place, as the image recreates.

The baths were also a noisy and rather disorderly place. People ate and drank there, as shown by a graffito from Herculaneum that notes food prices in asses, there were fights and crowds, and some graffiti recall that people also sought sex and that prostitution was practised. The most frequent problem was the theft of clothes, which bathers left in the changing room in the care of a slave, which is why at the baths of Bath (Britannia) curse tablets against thieves were found (Fagan, 1999).

title: The rooms of the baths
paras: Rome, 1st-3rd centuries AD

The diagram follows the bather's route through an imperial bathhouse. He left his clothes in the apodyterium, the changing room, in small niches watched over by a slave, and went out into the palaestra, the porticoed courtyard where exercise before bathing took place. There people lifted weights, practised wrestling and played ball games.

After exercise he sweated in the laconicum, the steam room, moved on to the caldarium, with its tubs of hot water, went back to the tepidarium, a transitional room, and finished in the frigidarium, with those of cold water. The great baths also had reading rooms, so the bath could end among books.

The presence of balls was common in the baths. The Greek physician Galen (2nd century AD) devoted an entire treatise, De parvae pilae exercitio, to defending this game as the best bodily activity. According to him, it moved the whole body with whatever intensity one wished, suited any age and cost hardly any money, so it was within the reach even of the poor. Moreover, unlike wrestling, it also trained the mind, because it forced players to anticipate the opponent's movements, and it rarely caused injuries.

title: Roman balls
paras: Rome, 1st-2nd centuries AD

Pila paganica. This was the most common ball, stuffed with feathers, and it was played by keeping it from falling or passing it with or without a bounce. The poet Martial describes it as neither as soft as the follis nor as hard as the ordinary pila, and the one in the upper image is a modern reconstruction.

Follis. This was a larger ball, of inflated skin, very light and suited to children and the elderly, like the one in the drawing in the lower image. It was made from an inflated pig's bladder covered with leather, and children warmed it by the fire to round it out. Even so, adults used it too, and Augustus, after the civil wars, exchanged exercises with weapons for the ball and the follis.

title: Trigon and harpastum
paras: Rome, 1st-5th centuries AD

Pila trigonalis. A popular game in which three players (trigonali) stood forming a triangle (trigon). The idea was to pass a small ball hard to test the reflexes of a team-mate, who had to catch it without letting it fall, and perhaps several balls at once were used. In wealthy houses the slaves who were given the name of pilicrepus replaced the balls and kept count of the points.

Harpastum. It was played with a small, hard and somewhat heavy ball. Its violent variant, presumably used to train the Roman legions, was a team game in which the ball had to be carried to the end of the playing area by any means (tackles, punches, kicks, etc.) (Tanyeri & Sezik Tanyeri, 2026).

In its more peaceful form, it was a game in which a player standing in the middle tried to intercept the ball that the others passed to one another, and it required speed and reflexes. Some women also played it, among them Philaenis, whom the poet Martial mocks.

Women playing ball appear above all in a mosaic from the Villa del Casale, at Piazza Armerina (Sicily), from the first half of the 4th century AD (left-hand image), which decorated a room in the private part of the villa. Even so, women's sport was an uncommon practice in Rome, since a woman exercising outside the home was considered improper.

The girls in the mosaic wear briefs and a band across the chest, the strophium, with which sportswomen covered themselves, which is why popular accounts have called them the «bikini girls» (Muñoz-Santos, 2017). Some play ball, and others run, throw the discus or prepare for the jump with halteres, while the winners receive the palm and the crown of victory.

The scene was at first taken for a beauty contest and is today interpreted as an athletic competition (Pensabene & Gallocchio, 2011). This source shows that, at least in the late imperial period, upper-class women had more open access to sporting practice, essentially in private settings. It is also striking that their events were those of Greek athletics, the foot race, the jump and the discus, which Rome had known for centuries.

title: Athletics in Rome
paras: Rome, 186 BC-3rd century AD

Greek athletics reached Rome in 186 BC, when a victorious general offered, according to the historian Livy, the first contest of athletes brought from Greece together with a hunt of lions and panthers. During the Republic it was an occasional display among other spectacles that the Roman watched from the stands, since undressing before one's fellow citizens was considered shameful.

The emperor Domitian (AD 81-96) gave it a home of its own with this stadium, built for the Capitoline Games, a Greek-style contest that he instituted in AD 86, held every four years and, according to the biographer Suetonius, included a girls' race. It was the first permanent stadium in Rome, with some 30,000 spectators.

The shape of the building recalled that of a smaller circus (right-hand image). The track measured some 192 metres, the length of the Greek stadium, and besides athletics it hosted boxing, pankration and, probably, gladiators after the fire in the Colosseum in AD 217. Its site is now occupied by Piazza Navona, which preserves its shape.

title: The criticism of the spectacles
paras: Rome and Africa, 1st century BC-5th century AD
The chart compares, point by point, the two criticisms the spectacles received, that of the pagan moralists, on the left, and that of the Christian writers, on the right.

The first arose within the Roman elite itself. Cicero wondered what pleasure a cultivated man could find in wild-beast hunts, and the philosopher Seneca describes the midday session, when those left in the stands shouted at the condemned man «Kill him, flog him, burn him!». His complaint was aimed at violence against those who could not defend themselves, since he accepted the arena as a punishment, and it was addressed to the cultivated man so that he would not be carried away by the taste of the masses.

Christian writers attacked the games for idolatry. Tertullian wrote between AD 197 and 200 De spectaculis, in which he recalled that everything in them was consecrated to the pagan gods, called the opening procession the «procession of Satan» (pompa diaboli) and reproached the public for their betting and their euphoria over the winning charioteer. Two centuries later, Augustine of Hippo maintained the condemnation, although he admitted that a Christian might enter the amphitheatre if by doing so he freed a gladiator.

Neither of the two closed down the spectacles, since the pagan one sought only to keep the cultivated man away from the stands and the Church spoke to its faithful without any power over the venues. The end, therefore, came by other routes.

title: How the spectacles faded away
paras: West and East, 4th-6th centuries AD

Roman spectacles were not banned in any particular year. In the West no law put an end to them, so each spectacle followed its own chronology. Gladiatorial combats were the first to disappear: by the end of the 4th century they took up in Rome only ten days in December, and the last was probably held c. 440.

The main cause was money. From the 3rd century the cities grew poorer, and the rich who had once paid for the games devoted their generosity to churches, hospitals and almsgiving, which the bishops presented as the new way to earn recognition. Christianity rejected the violence of the arena, although Jiménez Sánchez (2002) considers its weight exaggerated and puts cost first, since gladiatorial combat was the most expensive spectacle. Stocking (2021) agrees that Christianity was not the main cause.

Hunts and races, cheaper and more popular, lasted longer. After the fall of the Western Empire in 476, the Germanic kings of Italy kept up the games, and there the last documented hunt dates from 523 and the last race from 549.

In the East, by contrast, the emperor went on paying, and the hippodrome of Constantinople kept up the races and the factions for centuries (Giatsis, 2000; Parnell, 2014). The spectacle was a service paid for by those in power, and it faded out wherever they stopped paying for it.

title: The functions of Roman sport and its legacy
paras: Throughout the topic, Roman sport has appeared linked to four spheres of city life, power, the social order, religion and health, and in all of them the distance from the Greek agon can be seen, because in Rome the game offered to the public took precedence over competition between the participants.

First, sport served power. The elite offered games to the plebs on a regular and free basis to win its favour, the rich man who paid for them received recognition in return (euergetism) and the emperor showed himself in the stands as the one who gave the games and granted what was asked of him.

Second, sport ordered society, since the stands reproduced the hierarchy of the city and whoever displayed himself for money was branded with infamia, which is why in the arena and the circus those who competed were above all slaves, the condemned and professionals while the citizen watched from the stands, as in Etruria.
Third, it was a rite, since the ludi belonged to the religious calendar and the circus remained a sacred space, which is why the Christians condemned it.
Finally, daily exercise served health in the baths, open to anyone for a token price, in ball games and in youth associations, and Galen set out its rules.

What was passed on to the Middle Ages were, above all, the practices that did not depend on a payer. The warrior aristocracy of the Germanic kingdoms kept hunting and exercises on horseback as preparation for war and a sign of rank, the people kept up ball games and games of strength at their festivals, and the Church, which had condemned the spectacle, came to set the festive calendar. Sport ceased to be a spectacle that the city offered to the stands and became a group practice, that of the nobles, that of the peasants and that of the clergy.
